# SRJ Consulting & Services LLC

> Operator-led AI advisory that recovers hidden AI spend, eliminates shadow AI risk, and turns scattered AI tools into a managed business function. Built for executives at organizations from 20 to 1,000 employees who are accountable for AI outcomes but lack the operating discipline to manage them. Founded by Stephen R. Jordan, licensed attorney, drawing on three decades of senior security and operations leadership at Citi, Intel, McAfee, and Optiv.

## AI Governance Reference Library

The AI Governance Reference Library is a sixty-three-page reference covering every framework, law, agency enforcement posture, and sector rule that governs AI in the United States and the European Union, plus dedicated coverage of China and ten further jurisdictions (South Korea, Japan, Singapore, India, Canada, Brazil, the UK, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Australia). Each page answers the same four questions: what the framework actually is, what it requires of you, why it matters commercially and legally, and what a defensible position looks like. Every page carries a plain-language summary, a step-by-step compliance path, attributed findings from peer-reviewed research, and links to the primary sources. Written for executives, not lawyers.

Maintenance posture: the library is checked against primary sources rather than secondary summaries, and reviewed on a recurring cadence. Last reviewed 24 July 2026. Where a law has been repealed or a standard superseded, the page says so and explains what replaced it, rather than quietly deleting the entry. Four material changes were recorded at the July 2026 review: the Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205) was REPEALED by SB 26-189 on 14 May 2026 and never took effect; Federal Reserve SR 11-7 and OCC Bulletin 2011-12 were SUPERSEDED on 17 April 2026 by SR 26-2 and OCC Bulletin 2026-13; the EU AI Act Digital Omnibus was formally adopted on 29 June 2026, deferring Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027; NIST's Cyber AI Profile (IR 8596), COSAiS control overlays, and AI RMF Critical Infrastructure Profile are three distinct efforts that are frequently conflated; and the EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) was added as a new page, because its reporting duty bites on 11 September 2026 and reaches products already on the market, and because its Article 12 route to deemed compliance with EU AI Act Article 15 covers the CYBERSECURITY limb only. Accuracy and robustness remain live and must be evidenced independently. Almost every published summary of Article 12 drops the opening clause "without prejudice to the requirements relating to accuracy and robustness" and is therefore wrong on the point that matters most.

A second correction of the same kind was recorded on 14 July 2026, on the EU AI Act page. It is widely believed and widely written that a "high-risk" classification under the EU AI Act triggers a third-party conformity assessment. For the categories most businesses actually operate in, that is FALSE. Article 43(2) routes Annex III points 2 to 8 (critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services including credit scoring, law enforcement, migration, and justice) to the internal-control procedure under Annex VI, which the text states expressly "does not provide for the involvement of a notified body." A notified body is mandatory only for Annex III point 1 (biometrics), and only where the harmonised standards have not been applied in full, or where the AI is embedded in an Annex I Section A product and rides inside a sectoral assessment that already happens. Note also Article 43(6): the Commission may move points 2 to 8 onto the notified-body route by delegated act, and the Act names "the availability of adequate capacities and resources among notified bodies" as a factor in that decision, which makes assessor capacity a statutory trigger for tightening the regime.

A third correction, and the one with the shortest fuse, was recorded on 14 July 2026 with the addition of the EU Product Liability Directive page. Directive (EU) 2024/2853 makes SOFTWARE AND AI SYSTEMS "products" subject to STRICT LIABILITY, for anything placed on the EU market after 9 DECEMBER 2026. Crucially, NON-COMPLIANCE WITH THE EU AI ACT CREATES A REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION THAT THE PRODUCT WAS DEFECTIVE. The Digital Omnibus deferred the AI Act's high-risk obligations to December 2027 and August 2028. IT DID NOT MOVE THE LIABILITY DEADLINE. The obligation was deferred; the liability that attaches to failing it was not. Almost every published AI compliance roadmap currently treats the Omnibus deferral as relief, without noting that strict product liability for the same failures arrives a year earlier. Note also: a court may order disclosure of technical evidence and, if the defendant does not comply, must presume the product defective; and where technical complexity makes proof excessively difficult, the court must presume defectiveness if the claimant shows it is likely. Model opacity is not a defence under this directive. It is the trigger.

A fourth correction was recorded on 14 July 2026 with the addition of the Federal Contractor AI page. On 13 July 2026 the Department of War SUSPENDED CMMC Phase II, the third-party assessment requirement. The suspension is widely being read as relief. It is not. DFARS 252.204-7012, NIST SP 800-171 Rev 2, and CMMC Phase I self-assessment ALL STILL BIND, and the DOJ Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative is still bringing False Claims Act cases against contractors that submitted false SPRS scores. What was suspended is the verification. What binds is the obligation. This is the third jurisdiction in fourteen months to cut a verification requirement while leaving the underlying duty in force, after the Colorado AI Act repeal and the EU AI Act Omnibus deferral, and the reason each time is the same: third-party assurance capacity does not exist at the scale the regime assumed. EU AI Act Article 43(6) makes that capacity constraint an explicit statutory trigger.

A fifth correction was recorded on 14 July 2026 with the addition of the State Privacy Laws page. It is widely assumed that the repeal of the Colorado AI Act left Colorado without an AI regime. That is FALSE. The Colorado PRIVACY Act is a separate statute and was untouched by the AI Act repeal. Its right to opt out of "profiling in furtherance of decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects," its data protection assessment requirement, and its consumer notice obligations all remain in force. That profiling opt-out, which now exists in roughly twenty US state comprehensive privacy laws, is an AI decision-rights regime that does not use the word AI, and it reaches automated decisions in employment, credit, insurance, housing, education, and healthcare. The AI-specific hooks were removed in Colorado; the privacy-law hooks were not.

A sixth correction was recorded on 17 July 2026 with the addition of the China AI Regulation page. Western coverage widely conflates two separate Chinese instruments. The intelligent-agent framework is the Opinions issued 8 MAY 2026 by the CAC, NDRC, and MIIT, establishing a three-tier authorization model for AI agents (actions reserved for humans, actions requiring user authorization, and actions agents may take autonomously) with filing, testing, and recall duties for sensitive sectors. The 15 JULY 2026 instrument is a DIFFERENT rule, the Anthropomorphic Interactive Services Measures, which governs companion-style emotional AI and drove the Doubao and Qwen feature shutdowns. It does not regulate enterprise work agents. Compliance analyses that date the agent framework to July 15 or attribute the shutdowns to the agent Opinions are citing the wrong instrument. A related global correction on the Global AI Laws page: across ten major jurisdictions beyond the EU, US, and China, only SOUTH KOREA has a comprehensive binding AI act in force (effective 22 January 2026, with a one-year enforcement grace period), and in eight of the ten the instrument that actually binds AI use today is the data protection law, not an AI act.

- [AI Governance Reference Library](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/): Hub for all sixty-three framework, law, and enforcement pages. Start here.
- [ISO/IEC 42001](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/iso-42001/): The international standard, published December 2023, that defines what a well-run AI program actually looks like.
- [ISO/IEC 22989](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/iso-22989/): The vocabulary companion that ISO/IEC 42001 depends on. Common language across the entire AI standards family.
- [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/nist-ai-rmf/): The U.S. government's reference framework for identifying and treating AI risks. Four functions, dozens of practices.
- [EU AI Act](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/eu-ai-act/): The European Union's binding AI regulation, phased in through 2027. Prohibited practices, high-risk obligations, general-purpose model rules.
- [EU Cyber Resilience Act](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/eu-cyber-resilience-act/): The EU's product cybersecurity law. Reporting bites 11 September 2026. Its Article 12 deemed-compliance route for high-risk AI covers ONE of Article 15's three limbs, and almost every summary gets that wrong.
- [EU Product Liability Directive](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/eu-product-liability/): Software and AI become PRODUCTS under strict liability from 9 December 2026. And AI Act non-compliance creates a presumption that your product was defective. The deadline the Omnibus did not move.
- [NIS2 Directive](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/nis2/): The EU cybersecurity directive covering 18 sectors. Management bodies are PERSONALLY accountable, and executives of essential entities can be temporarily banned from management functions.
- [DORA](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/dora/): The EU financial sector ICT resilience regulation. Applicable since January 2025, now in its first real enforcement cycle. The management body owns ICT risk, and the duty is non-delegable.
- [NYDFS Part 500](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/nydfs-part-500/): New York's cybersecurity regulation, 23 NYCRR Part 500, fully phased in 1 November 2025. Its two AI industry letters (October 2024 and May 2026) add NO new requirements; they explain how the existing Part 500 program already reaches AI. The CEO-and-CISO annual certification is the pressure point.
- [Federal Contractor AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/federal-contractor-ai/): CMMC Phase II was SUSPENDED on 13 July 2026, but DFARS 252.204-7012, NIST SP 800-171, and Phase I self-assessment still bind, and False Claims Act enforcement continues. The verification was cut; the obligation was not.
- [State Privacy Laws](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/state-privacy-laws/): The profiling opt-out in roughly twenty state comprehensive privacy laws is an AI decision-rights regime that does not use the word AI. It survived the Colorado AI Act repeal untouched and reaches employment, credit, insurance, housing, education, and healthcare decisions.
- [CETS 225](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/coe-framework-convention/): The Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI, the first legally binding international AI treaty. In force 1 November 2025. The EU ratified 15 May 2026; the US signed but the Senate has not ratified. Not self-executing, so private-sector reach depends on each signatory's implementation.
- [China AI Regulation](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/china-ai-regulation/): China's AI instrument stack, and the two-instruments correction. The intelligent-agent Opinions of 8 May 2026 (three-tier authorization, sensitive-sector filing and recall) are a SEPARATE rule from the 15 July 2026 Anthropomorphic Interactive Services Measures that drove the Doubao and Qwen shutdowns. Enterprise work agents are governed by the former, not the latter.
- [Global AI Laws](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/global-ai-laws/): Ten jurisdictions beyond the EU, US, and China: South Korea, Japan, Singapore, India, Canada, Brazil, the UK, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Australia. Only South Korea has a binding comprehensive AI act in force. In eight of ten, the binding layer is privacy law, not an AI act.
- [New York City AI Laws](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/nyc-ai-laws/): NYC's automated employment decision tools law and the broader city-agency AI disclosure framework. Bias audits, notice, and public registries.
- [NYC Local Law 144](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/nyc-ai-laws/nyc-ll-144/): NYC's bias-audit and candidate-notification law for hiring tools.
- [NYC Local Law 35](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/nyc-ai-laws/nyc-ll-35/): NYC's ADS (Automated Decision Systems) framework for city agencies.
- [State AI Laws](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/state-ai-laws/): The state-by-state AI laws now in effect. Impact assessments, transparency, employment-decision rules, voice-and-likeness rights, consumer notification.
- [Colorado AI Act](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/state-ai-laws/colorado-ai-act/): REPEALED before it ever took effect. What SB 26-189 replaced it with, and why the repeal is the most instructive event in US state AI law.
- [Texas Responsible AI Governance Act](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/state-ai-laws/texas-ai-act/): Texas's AI governance framework, effective 2026. Impact assessments, developer duties, government use rules.
- [California AI Laws](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/state-ai-laws/california-ai-laws/): California's stack of AI laws covering training data disclosure, AI content labeling, healthcare AI, and generative AI.
- [Illinois AI Laws](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/state-ai-laws/illinois-ai-laws/): Illinois's AI video interview disclosure requirements and its employment AI restrictions under HB 3773.
- [Connecticut AI Act](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/state-ai-laws/connecticut-ai-act/): Connecticut's comprehensive AI law, Public Act 26-15 (the CART Act), signed May 27, 2026, with staggered effective dates from October 1, 2026 through January 1, 2028. Employment disclosure, frontier whistleblower protections, synthetic content watermarking, AI companion rules, anti-discrimination.
- [Tennessee ELVIS Act](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/state-ai-laws/tennessee-elvis-act/): Tennessee's voice-and-likeness rights law protecting artists and individuals from unauthorized AI imitation.
- [Federal AI Legislation](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/federal-ai-legislation/): The federal AI bills in play, what they would do if passed, and the operating posture you should hold while they develop.
- [SR 11-7 and the 2026 Model Risk Guidance](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sr-11-7/): SUPERSEDED in April 2026 by SR 26-2 and OCC Bulletin 2026-13. What the revised interagency model risk guidance changes for AI.
- [Agency Enforcement](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/agency-enforcement/): The federal agencies actively enforcing existing laws against AI misuse. Anti-AI-washing, disparate impact, adverse action, registrant governance.
- [FTC AI Enforcement](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/agency-enforcement/ftc-ai-enforcement/): The Federal Trade Commission's active AI enforcement posture. AI-washing, deceptive claims, unfairness.
- [EEOC AI Enforcement](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/agency-enforcement/eeoc-ai-enforcement/): The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's enforcement of Title VII, ADEA, ADA, and GINA against AI-driven employment decisions.
- [CFPB AI Enforcement](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/agency-enforcement/cfpb-ai-enforcement/): The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's AI enforcement covering credit, lending, and financial products.
- [SEC AI Enforcement](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/agency-enforcement/sec-ai-enforcement/): The Securities and Exchange Commission's AI-washing enforcement and disclosure requirements for public registrants.
- [HHS OCR AI Enforcement](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/agency-enforcement/hhs-ocr-ai-enforcement/): The Office for Civil Rights within HHS enforcing HIPAA and Section 1557 against AI in healthcare.
- [Sector Rules](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sector-rules/): The pre-existing federal statutes and regulations that now govern how AI can be used in regulated sectors. Data handling, adverse action, disparate impact.
- [HIPAA and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sector-rules/hipaa-ai/): How HIPAA governs AI when it touches protected health information. Business associates, safeguards, breach notification.
- [COPPA and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sector-rules/coppa-ai/): How COPPA governs AI when children under 13 are involved. Verifiable parental consent, data minimization, deletion rights.
- [GDPR and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sector-rules/gdpr-ai/): How the General Data Protection Regulation governs AI systems processing EU personal data. Automated decisions, DPIAs, lawful bases.
- [GLBA and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sector-rules/glba-ai/): How the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act governs AI at financial institutions. Safeguards Rule, Privacy Rule, third-party oversight.
- [FCRA and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sector-rules/fcra-ai/): How the Fair Credit Reporting Act governs AI that produces consumer reports. Accuracy, adverse action notices, dispute rights.
- [ECOA and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sector-rules/ecoa-ai/): How the Equal Credit Opportunity Act governs AI in lending. Adverse action, disparate impact, specific reasons.
- [Title VII and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sector-rules/title-vii-ai/): How Title VII of the Civil Rights Act governs AI in employment. Disparate impact, disparate treatment, business necessity.
- [WARN Act and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sector-rules/warn-ai/): How the WARN Act governs mass layoffs, including AI-driven workforce reductions. Notice periods, covered employers, exceptions.
- [FERPA and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sector-rules/ferpa-ai/): How FERPA governs AI that touches student education records. The school official exception under 34 CFR 99.31(a)(1) is the only workable path for most EdTech AI, and most vendor contracts do not actually satisfy its direct-control requirement.
- [FINRA and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sector-rules/finra-ai/): FINRA has issued no AI rule. Its position is that Rule 3110 supervision, Rule 4511 books and records, Reg BI, and the Rule 2210 communications rules already apply to AI, and that a broker-dealer that cannot supervise an AI system is not permitted to use it.
- [Financial Reporting Rules for AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/financial-reporting/): The accounting and audit rules that govern how AI shows up in financial reporting. Software cost accounting, ICFR, audit committee oversight.
- [FASB ASU 2025-06](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/financial-reporting/fasb-asu-2025-06/): The Financial Accounting Standards Board update on software cost accounting for AI implementations.
- [AICPA AI Guidance](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/financial-reporting/aicpa-ai-guidance/): The American Institute of CPAs' guidance for auditors on how to assess AI use by clients.
- [PCAOB AI Guidance](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/financial-reporting/pcaob-ai-guidance/): The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board's guidance on AI in public company audits.
- [SOX 302 and 404 for AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/financial-reporting/sox-302-404-ai/): How Sarbanes-Oxley Sections 302 and 404 govern AI in internal control over financial reporting (ICFR).
- [Director Oversight](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/director-oversight/): The fiduciary duty of directors to oversee material risk categories, now applied to AI. What boards must actually do.
- [General Business Governance](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/general-business-governance/): The pre-existing control frameworks that layer beneath AI governance but do not substitute for it.
- [ISO 27001 and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/general-business-governance/iso-27001-ai/): How ISO 27001 information security controls apply to AI systems and where they fall short.
- [SOC 2 and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/general-business-governance/soc-2-ai/): How SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, confidentiality, processing integrity, privacy) apply to AI providers.
- [NIST Cybersecurity Framework and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/general-business-governance/nist-csf-ai/): How the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover, Govern) applies to AI systems.
- [COSO ERM and AI](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/general-business-governance/coso-erm-ai/): How the COSO Enterprise Risk Management framework covers AI risks and where AI needs its own layer.
- [Vendor Disclosure](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/vendor-disclosure/): The emerging standards for what vendors must disclose about the software and AI components they supply. SBOM and AIBOM.
- [Software Bill of Materials](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/vendor-disclosure/sbom/): What an SBOM is, what it contains, and what buyers now require in vendor contracts.
- [AI Bill of Materials](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/vendor-disclosure/aibom/): What an AIBOM is, what it discloses about AI models and training data, and what buyers should require.
- [Data Management Frameworks](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/data-management-frameworks/): The underlying data-management discipline on which AI governance sits. Knowledge areas, cloud data controls, capability maturity.
- [DAMA-DMBOK](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/data-management-frameworks/dama-dmbok/): The reference body of knowledge for data management. Eleven knowledge areas covering the discipline AI governance sits on.
- [EDM Council DCAM](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/data-management-frameworks/dcam/): The EDM Council's capability model for measuring data management maturity, widely used in financial services.
- [CDMC Cloud Data Management](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/data-management-frameworks/cdmc/): The EDM Council's cloud data management framework. Fourteen key controls for cloud data security and governance.
- [AI Tools](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/ai-tools/): A reference catalog of 320 AI tools across 23 categories, each listed with vendor, official vendor URL, headquarters jurisdiction, and the governance flag it raises, from recording consent to source-code exposure to cross-border data review. The working list behind an AI tool inventory, the first artifact of AI governance.
- [Sources & References](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-governance/sources/): The complete bibliography of the library: 78 primary sources (statutes, regulators, standards bodies, official publications) and 45 peer-reviewed or formally published research works, in one place, maintained the way a book maintains its reference section.

- [The AI IT Security Implementation & Strategy(TM)](https://srjconsultingservices.com/services/risk-governance-security/ai-security-implementation/): Implementation framework for executive-led AI security programs.
- [Secure by Design in the Age of AI(TM)](https://srjconsultingservices.com/services/risk-governance-security/secure-by-design/): Embeds security into AI product development from the first architecture decision, before insecure patterns harden into the product.
- [Application Security in the Age of AI(TM)](https://srjconsultingservices.com/services/risk-governance-security/application-security/): Secures AI-powered applications in production, where runtime behavior is non-deterministic and traditional AppSec assumptions break.
- [Cloud and Infrastructure Security in the Age of AI(TM)](https://srjconsultingservices.com/services/risk-governance-security/cloud-infrastructure-security/): Secures the cloud and infrastructure layer that AI workloads run on, including data sovereignty and control-plane exposure.

## Applications

- [Applications Hub](https://srjconsultingservices.com/applications/): The Operating Discipline for AI Library(TM) packaged as operationalized products. Each application takes a framework from the book series and packages it as a structured questionnaire that produces a scored report leadership can put in front of a board, an auditor, an acquirer, or an insurance carrier. Deterministic scoring rubric, no model-in-the-loop guessing, the same answers always produce the same score.
- [The AI Audit](https://srjconsultingservices.com/ai-audit/): Application 01, LIVE. Five-dimension audit that surfaces what unmanaged AI is silently costing the business across tool inventory, cost mapping, performance measurement, risk exposure, and governance gaps. The cumulative cost of unmanaged AI across mid-market operators averages roughly $670,000 per year; the audit produces the specific number for your business. Tier 1 Snapshot is $399 one-time at aiauditforcompanies.com/startaiaudit/. Built directly on The Operating Discipline for AI Library(TM).
- [Outcomestar](https://srjconsultingservices.com/applications/outcomestar/): Application 02. A structured family record product built on the same operating logic as The AI Audit: methodology first, application second, defensible output third.

- [Application Security in the Age of AI(TM)](https://srjconsultingservices.com/books/ai-risk-governance-security/the-application-security/): Book 08 of 9, Book 4 of 5 in AI Risk Governance & Security(TM). Securing AI applications in production. Forthcoming.
